notes: The starting point of “the thirtieth year” is not stated. Verse 2 gives a separate date relative to Jehoiachin’s exile.
The identifications of the gleaming metal and gemstones are uncertain. “Sapphire” may denote lapis lazuli. These are comparisons describing the vision’s appearance.

Verse 15 compresses the relation between the wheel and the four faces; the translation reads it distributively, in light of the four wheels in verse 16. Verse 23 repeats the phrase about two wings covering the body.
vocabulary: Likeness
Hebrew demut qualifies what Ezekiel sees; the repeated word keeps resemblance distinct from exact identification.
Spirit
Hebrew ruach can mean wind, breath, or spirit. Its use connects the creatures’ movement with the wheels without explaining the vision’s mechanics.

notes: The Hebrew calls Israel “rebellious nations,” using an unexpected plural. The translation preserves it.
vocabulary: Son of man
Hebrew ben-adam, literally “son of a human.” This recurring address stresses Ezekiel’s humanity; here it is an address to the prophet, not a separate figure in the vision.
Lord GOD
Hebrew Adonai YHWH. GOD in capitals represents the divine name, conventionally rendered LORD when it stands alone.

notes: The pinned Hebrew reads “Blessed be the glory of the LORD from his place.” The translation retains this blessing rather than changing the consonants to describe the glory rising.
The text explicitly makes God the one who puts the stumbling block before the person. It does not explain away the tension between this action and the person’s responsibility.
vocabulary: Adamant
A very hard substance; its precise identification is uncertain. The comparison emphasizes hardness greater than flint.
Watchman
A lookout responsible for warning of danger. Verses 18–21 apply that responsibility to the prophet’s speech.

notes: The pinned Hebrew assigns 390 days to Israel and forty to Judah, one day for a year. It does not identify a starting date for calculating those years.
Dung is the fuel used to bake the bread, not an ingredient. The concession changes human dung to cattle dung.
vocabulary: Shekel; hin
A shekel is a weight and a hin a liquid measure. These small daily rations enact shortage; ancient values should not be treated as exact modern measurements.
Staff of bread
An image of food as the support of life. Breaking it means removing that support.

notes: The Hebrew says the people have not followed the surrounding nations’ judgments. This negative is retained; 11:12 makes a different accusation.
“Cut you down” renders a verb meaning diminish or take away. Its object is unstated; “withdraw” is another possible understanding.
vocabulary: Sign action
The shaved hair is divided into thirds, while even a few hairs initially preserved are exposed to fire. The following speech interprets the action.

notes: “I was broken by” follows the passive Hebrew form. The syntax is difficult; another interpretation understands God as breaking the people’s unfaithful heart.
The pinned text names Diblah. Its location is uncertain; the translation does not silently replace it with Riblah. The phrase may also compare the desolation with a wilderness toward Diblah.
vocabulary: High places
Hebrew bamot, sites of worship. The surrounding references to altars and idols identify their role here.

notes: Several expressions are difficult. Verse 5 literally has “disaster, one disaster.” The rare word rendered “doom” can also be understood as a turn or cycle; the mountain sound and final terms in verse 11 are uncertain. The repeated arrival of judgment remains clear.
Literally, “all knees will go with water.” The image may describe weakness or water running down the legs through loss of bladder control in terror.
The beautiful ornament may be jewelry or the temple’s splendor. The translation follows the ornament/treasure reading while retaining the sacred place in verse 22.
vocabulary: Unclean
The word can refer to ritual impurity. Wealth once prized is now treated as something to discard.

notes: The pinned Hebrew reads “fire.” A reading “man” is sometimes proposed because of the human form in the vision; it is not adopted here.
The Hebrew says “to be far from my sanctuary” without an explicit subject. The translation understands the abominations as driving God away; it can also describe the people’s distancing themselves.
The meaning of putting a branch to their noses is uncertain. The translation preserves the gesture without reconstructing a ritual or obscenity.
vocabulary: Image of jealousy
An image that provokes divine jealousy. The text does not identify the deity represented.
Tammuz
A named deity mourned by the women in this vision. The verse does not describe the full rite.

notes: Six armed men appear, with a linen-clad man “among them.” The wording does not explicitly settle whether the linen-clad man is counted among the six.
The vision names the killing of children as well as adults and then records Ezekiel’s anguished protest. Both are retained without turning the account into a general instruction.
vocabulary: Mark
Hebrew taw, “mark,” also the name of a Hebrew letter. The text identifies its protective function but does not specify a theological interpretation of its shape.

notes: The first face is called a cherub’s face here, while 1:10 names an ox’s face. The translation keeps the difference even though verses 20–22 identify the creatures as the same ones.
vocabulary: Cherubim
Plural of cherub. These are the living creatures Ezekiel identifies in verse 20, not the small winged children familiar from later art.
Whirling wheels
Hebrew galgal distinguishes the revolving wheelwork from the ordinary word for a wheel, ofan.

sections.18: The glory at the east gate

notes: The first clause is difficult. It can be read as a statement, “The time to build houses is not near,” or as a question, “Is it not time to build houses?” The pot-and-meat saying is answered in verses 7–11.
“Nor” carries the first clause’s negative into the coordinated second clause. The Hebrew has no second explicit negative.
“For a little while” can also mean “in small measure.” Verse 19 retains the Hebrew’s shift from “them” to “you” and its “one heart,” rather than replacing it with “a new heart.”
vocabulary: Heart of flesh
A living heart contrasted with stone. “Flesh” here does not itself mean moral corruption.

notes: The prince is brought to Babylon yet will not see it. The translation leaves that tension in place rather than inserting an explanation from another narrative.
vocabulary: Burden
Hebrew massa can refer to a load or a prophetic pronouncement; here the word connects the message to the belongings carried in the sign.
Divination
Seeking or claiming hidden knowledge. The speech qualifies this divination as flattering.

notes: The coating may be whitewash or inadequate plaster or mortar. The image exposes reassurance that cannot make a failing wall sound.

The objects called bands and veils and the actions involving them are uncertain. Verse 18 literally has “all the joints of my arms,” an anomalous first-person expression; “every wrist” follows the apparent bodily setting. The repeated “flying” language in verse 20 is rendered “like birds.” These details require further specialist review.
vocabulary: Daughters of your people
The women addressed are accused of prophesying from their own hearts, parallel to the men in verse 2. Their gender remains explicit.

notes: The Hebrew repeats the same verb for the prophet being deceived and God deceiving him. The translation preserves that attribution; the passage also holds prophet and inquirer accountable.

The written form is Danel; the reading tradition supplied in the pinned source has Daniel. The identity of the figure is disputed. The translation follows the supplied reading without settling that identification.
vocabulary: Stumbling block of guilt
An image for what draws a person into guilt; here it is placed before the face as idols are raised in the heart.

notes: The comparison concerns vine wood’s usefulness for making objects, not the value of grapes. Adding fruitfulness here would change the argument.
vocabulary: Unfaithfulness
Hebrew maal describes a breach of trust or obligation. The land’s desolation is linked to that breach.

notes: Jerusalem, Samaria, and Sodom are personified as female relatives. Their “daughters” are associated communities. Left and right correspond to north and south when facing east; the parentage belongs to the allegory.

“Full womanhood” renders the difficult phrase literally meaning “ornament of ornaments” in a context of bodily maturation. The animal skin and costly textile in verse 10 are also uncertain; no precise species or fabric is asserted.
“Through the fire” supplies the setting of the passing-over expression from the child-sacrifice context; “fire” is not explicit in this verse, though it is in 20:31.

Verse 26 literally calls the Egyptians “great of flesh,” understood sexually here. The heart expression in verse 30 is uncertain, variously understood as weak, feverish, or impetuous. The noun in verse 36 ordinarily means copper; “lust” is a contextual interpretation, while expenditure of wealth is another possibility.

The last clause of verse 43 is rendered as a rhetorical question; it can instead be read as a prohibition against further lewdness. Verse 47’s short phrase about “little” is understood to intensify the comparison with the sisters.
vocabulary: Covenant
The relationship sworn in verse 8 is remembered and reestablished in verses 60–63. The translation retains both the covenant and the difficult statements about shame and atonement.

notes: “Land of merchants” uses a word also associated with Canaan. In verse 21 the pinned reading is “fugitives”; the translation does not substitute the proposed reading “chosen troops.”
vocabulary: Riddle; parable
The image is presented before its interpretation. Verses 12–21 name the political actors; verses 22–24 return to the tree image without naming a later individual.
Gave his hand
A gesture of pledge or agreement. Its force is explained by the surrounding oath and covenant language.

notes: The Hebrew in verse 10 contains a difficult word normally meaning “brother.” The translation follows the apparent sense “any of these things.” Verse 11’s pronouns are clarified as father and son; another reading takes the opening clause as the son’s failure to do the righteous acts.
The pinned text says he withdraws his hand “from the poor.” The translation supplies “harming” to express restraint; it does not replace “poor” with the proposed reading “injustice.”
vocabulary: Life; person
Hebrew nephesh names the living person here. The same word underlies both the assertion that lives belong to God and the statement about the person who sins.
New heart and new spirit
Here the people are commanded to make these for themselves. The gift language in 11:19 is retained there; the different emphases are not harmonized.

notes: The pinned Hebrew has “he knew his widows,” an obscure expression. The translation retains his widows and the verb “knew”; other readings understand sexual violation or propose “ravaged their strongholds.” The precise meaning remains unresolved.
“In your blood” is the wording of the pinned Hebrew and is obscure here. Readings such as “in your vineyard” require a textual change. The surrounding description of a well-watered vine is clear.
vocabulary: Lament
Hebrew qinah identifies the poem’s mourning form. The lion cubs and vine branches portray rulers without supplying their personal names.

notes: The text directly attributes not-good statutes and defilement through offerings to God. These claims remain alongside the accusations of rebellion. “Through the fire” in verse 26 is supplied from the explicit wording in verse 31.
Bamah means “high place”; the question plays on its sound. Verse 39 can be read as an assurance of future listening, as here, or as a conditional refusal to listen; the Hebrew is compressed.
These verses correspond to 21:1–5 in the pinned Hebrew numbering. Public chapter 21 begins at Hebrew 21:6.
vocabulary: Raised my hand
A repeated oath gesture. Retaining the hand language links the promises and judgments across the chapter.

notes: Public verses 1–32 correspond to Hebrew 21:6–37. The source records are bound in full, including their numbering annotations.

The sword poem contains several difficult expressions, particularly the relation of the sword to “the scepter of my son” and the wording about testing. “Scepter” can also be “rod.” The translation retains the unresolved imagery; its syntax and the rare term in verse 15 need specialist review.

The parties to the oaths in verse 23 are not explicit. “Profane” in verse 25 can also be “slain” or “mortally wounded.” Verse 27 can refer to the one to whom judgment or the right belongs, without naming that person. The addressee shifts between sword and those judged in verses 29–30.
vocabulary: Bodily grief
Verse 6 literally speaks of broken loins. The water at the knees in verse 7 repeats the image in 7:17.
Teraphim
Cultic images used here in divination, alongside arrows and examination of a liver.

notes: “Uncovering a father’s nakedness” is a sexual kinship idiom. The verbs describing treatment of the menstruating woman and the sister convey violation or humiliation; the translation does not neutralize them as ordinary consensual relations.

Verse 16 is difficult; “be profaned” is followed here rather than an interpretation involving possession. Verse 25 reads “prophets” in the pinned text; “princes” is a proposed alternative not adopted here.
vocabulary: Holy/common; unclean/clean
These are two distinct contrasts in the priestly instruction, not interchangeable pairs.

notes: The sisters are explicitly identified as Samaria and Jerusalem. The sexual and violent imagery remains directed at personified cities. Verse 20’s donkey and horse comparisons refer to sexual organs and emissions.

The term “nearby” can also be understood as those who approach. The equipment word at the beginning of verse 24 is uncertain. Verse 34’s action toward the cup’s shards is difficult, often understood as gnawing or breaking; the tearing of breasts is explicit.

Fire is supplied in verse 37 from the child-sacrifice context. Verse 42’s word can be understood as drinkers or as Sabeans. Verse 43 follows the supplied plural reading “they will prostitute themselves,” but its final syntax is highly compressed.
vocabulary: Oholah; Oholibah
The names mean approximately “her tent” and “my tent is in her.” The text itself provides the corresponding city names.

notes: Verse 5 says “bones” beneath the pot; “wood” is a proposed correction, not the pinned wording. The cooking command in verse 10 and the wearying effort in verse 12 are difficult; the broader image is of cooking followed by an unsuccessful attempt to remove corrosion.

The death of Ezekiel’s wife and the restrictions on mourning are stated starkly. The text does not give her name or describe her response. Verse 22’s “as I have done” refers to Ezekiel’s actions within his report of the divine message.
vocabulary: Mourning customs
The listed headwear, footwear, lip covering, and food concern outward practices of mourning. The command to groan silently does not say that Ezekiel feels no grief.

sections.25: The fugitive and the opened mouth
